cards.definition_en: A way of protecting data in which the same secret key is used both to lock it and to unlock it.
examples: Symmetric encryption is fast, so it protects the bulk of the data in a connection.
Both sides need the same key for symmetric encryption, which is the hard part.
common_mistakes: Thinking symmetric means the data is encrypted twice.
Sending the shared key over the same insecure channel as the data.

cards.definition_en: A way of protecting data with a pair of linked keys: what one key locks, only the other key can unlock.
examples: Asymmetric encryption lets strangers send secrets without agreeing on a password first.
Because asymmetric encryption is slow, it is mostly used to exchange a symmetric key.
common_mistakes: Saying that the private key is used to encrypt for others: others use the public key.
Believing it is always better than symmetric encryption: it is slower.

cards.definition_en: The half of a key pair that its owner can share with anyone, used to lock data for the owner or to check the owner's signatures.
examples: Anyone can encrypt a message with her public key, but only she can read it.
The server sends its public key during the handshake.
common_mistakes: Thinking a public key must be kept secret.
Using 'open key' as a translation from Russian.

cards.definition_en: The secret half of a key pair that its owner never shares, used to unlock data or to create signatures.
examples: If the private key leaks, every message sent to its owner can be read.
The private key never leaves the hardware token.
common_mistakes: Emailing the private key to a colleague for convenience.
Mixing it up with the shared secret of symmetric encryption.

cards.definition_en: A defined method for turning readable data into unreadable data and back again using a key.
examples: Old servers still offered a weak cipher that attackers could break.
AES is a widely used cipher.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym of the process of encrypting: the cipher is the algorithm, encryption is the action.
Misspelling it as 'ciper' or 'sipher'.

cards.definition_en: Data in its readable form before it is encrypted or after it is decrypted; it does not have to be text.
examples: Storing a plaintext password in the database is a serious mistake.
The cipher turns plaintext into unreadable data.
common_mistakes: Thinking plaintext must be a text file: it can be an image or any data.
Writing it as two words, 'plain text', for the cryptographic term.

cards.definition_en: The unreadable result of encrypting data, which cannot be understood without the right key.
examples: An observer who sees only the ciphertext should learn nothing about the message.
The ciphertext is stored together with the initialization vector.
common_mistakes: Treating it as a hash: ciphertext can be turned back into the original with the key.
Assuming ciphertext is always printable text: it is usually binary data.

cards.definition_en: A procedure in which two parties agree on a shared secret over a channel that others may be watching.
examples: The key exchange happens at the start of every secure connection.
A signed key exchange prevents an attacker from taking part in the middle.
common_mistakes: Imagining that the key itself is sent in clear text.
Skipping authentication, which lets an attacker take part in the exchange.

cards.definition_en: A value made with a private key that shows who created some data and that the data has not been changed.
examples: The installer carries a digital signature from the software vendor.
Changing even one byte makes the digital signature invalid.
common_mistakes: Thinking it is an image of a handwritten signature.
Believing it encrypts the whole document: it proves origin and integrity.

cards.definition_en: A digital document that links a public key to the identity of its owner and is vouched for by a trusted organization.
examples: The browser warned that the certificate had expired yesterday.
The certificate contains the public key and the domain name of the site.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'sertificate' or 'certifcate'.
Confusing a certificate with a private key: it holds only public information.

cards.definition_en: An organization that browsers and systems trust to check who owns a domain or key and to issue a certificate for it.
examples: A certificate authority issued the certificate after checking control of the domain.
If a certificate authority is compromised, fake certificates can be created.
common_mistakes: Confusing the certificate authority with the owner of the website.
Thinking that the authority stores the private keys of its customers.

cards.definition_en: Random data added to a password before it is hashed, so equal passwords give different results and prepared lookup tables are useless.
examples: Each user gets a different salt, so two identical passwords do not share a hash.
The salt is stored next to the hash and does not need to be secret.
common_mistakes: Thinking the salt must be secret.
Using one fixed salt for all users.

cards.definition_en: A value that must be used only once with a given key in a protocol or encryption mode; repeating it can break security.
examples: Reusing a nonce with the same key can reveal the secret message.
The server sends a fresh nonce for every login attempt.
common_mistakes: Mixing it up with salt: a salt makes password hashes different, a nonce protects a single operation.
Thinking that a nonce has to be secret.

cards.definition_en: A starting value for certain encryption modes that makes the same plaintext produce different ciphertext each time.
examples: A new initialization vector is generated for every message.
The initialization vector is sent along with the ciphertext in the clear.
common_mistakes: Treating the initialization vector as a secret key.
Using the same initialization vector for every message.

cards.definition_en: An encryption method that works on data in fixed-size chunks, such as 128 bits at a time.
examples: AES is a block cipher that processes sixteen bytes at a time.
A block cipher needs a mode of operation to handle long messages safely.
common_mistakes: Using a block cipher in the simplest mode, which reveals repeated patterns.
Thinking a block cipher encrypts the whole file in one step.

cards.definition_en: An encryption method that mixes data with a continuous flow of pseudo-random bits, one piece at a time.
examples: A stream cipher is convenient when data arrives continuously.
Reusing the key and nonce in a stream cipher exposes the messages.
common_mistakes: Assuming a stream cipher is safe with any reused key.
Calling every cipher that handles long messages a stream cipher.

cards.definition_en: A small value calculated from data and used to notice accidental changes such as transmission errors.
examples: The download failed because the checksum did not match.
A simple checksum detects random errors but not deliberate tampering.
common_mistakes: Trusting a simple checksum to prove that no one altered a file on purpose.
Writing 'check sum' as two words.

cards.definition_en: A situation in which two different inputs produce exactly the same hash value.
examples: Researchers found a hash collision in an old algorithm, so it is no longer trusted.
A secure hash function makes a hash collision practically impossible to find.
common_mistakes: Believing that collisions cannot exist: they always exist in theory, but must be hard to find.
Writing 'colission' or 'collition'.

cards.definition_en: A protocol that encrypts the traffic between two programs and lets the client check the identity of the server; it is what makes HTTPS secure.
examples: The server accepts only modern versions of TLS.
A TLS handshake takes place before any web page is sent.
common_mistakes: Calling it SSL: SSL is the old, insecure predecessor.
Thinking TLS protects data stored on the server.

cards.definition_en: Protection of messages so that only the people communicating hold the keys, and even the service in between cannot read them.
examples: With end-to-end encryption the provider only stores unreadable data.
Backups can weaken end-to-end encryption if they are not protected.
common_mistakes: Thinking that an HTTPS connection to a server is end-to-end encryption.
Assuming the service can still recover messages after you forget the key.

cards.definition_en: Replacing cryptographic keys with new ones on a schedule or after a suspected leak.
examples: Key rotation limits how much data an attacker gets from one stolen key.
The team performs key rotation every ninety days.
common_mistakes: Changing the key but keeping the old one active forever.
Forgetting to re-encrypt old data when it is required.

cards.definition_en: A measure of how unpredictable a secret is; the more of it a password or key has, the harder it is to guess.
examples: A long random passphrase has more entropy than a short word with digits.
Virtual machines can lack entropy right after they start.
common_mistakes: Thinking that adding a digit to a common word gives high entropy.
Judging entropy by length alone: a long but predictable password still has low entropy.

cards.definition_en: An attack in which someone secretly places themselves between two parties and can read or change what they send.
examples: Certificate checks protect users from a man-in-the-middle attack.
A man-in-the-middle attack is easy on an open wireless network without encryption.
common_mistakes: Thinking the attacker must be physically inside the building.
Ignoring a browser warning about a certificate and letting the attack succeed.

cards.definition_en: A property of a connection that keeps old sessions private even if a long-term key is stolen later, because each session uses its own temporary keys.
examples: Thanks to forward secrecy, the stolen server key cannot decrypt last year's traffic.
Modern TLS configurations require forward secrecy.
common_mistakes: Thinking it protects against a stolen current session key.
Expecting it to help when the attacker already controls the server during the session.

cards.definition_en: A function that turns a password or another secret into one or more cryptographic keys; password-based ones such as Argon2 work slowly on purpose to make guessing expensive.
examples: A key derivation function with many iterations slows down password guessing.
Argon2 is a modern key derivation function.
common_mistakes: Using a fast general-purpose hash instead of a key derivation function for passwords.
Thinking it makes a weak password strong.
